description: Greek and Roman death rituals — the prothesis, ekphora, stelai and the Roman festivals for the dead.
content_html:
Why Burial Mattered

For ancient Greeks and Romans, proper burial was not a formality — it was a religious and moral necessity. The unburied dead were believed to wander the banks of the underworld rivers, unable to cross into the realm of Hades until their body had received the correct rites. Sophocles’ tragedy Antigone turns on this very point: Antigone defies the king’s edict in order to bury her brother, because leaving him unburied would condemn his soul to restless wandering. The obligation to bury the dead — and to bury them correctly — was one of the most powerful moral imperatives in the ancient world.

Greek Funeral Customs: The Prothesis

The Greek funeral followed a set sequence of three stages. The first was the prothesis — the laying-out of the body. Once someone died, the women of the household washed the body, anointed it with oil, dressed it in grave clothes, and placed it on a bier or low table in the entrance hall of the house, with the feet pointing towards the door. The body was wreathed with garlands. Family and friends gathered to lament, with women performing formal ritualised mourning — wailing, beating their breasts and tearing their hair. Athens eventually passed laws limiting the extremes of this mourning behaviour, suggesting it had become a competitive display of grief among wealthy families.

Evidence for the prothesis comes from surviving painted pottery. Attic geometric-period pottery from the 8th century BC shows schematic but unmistakeable scenes of the prothesis: the body laid horizontally on a bier, surrounded by rows of stylised mourning figures, with arms raised in the gesture of lamentation. These vessels were themselves often grave goods, placed in the tomb alongside the deceased.

Key Fact

The three stages of a Greek funeral: (1) Prothesis — the preparation and laying-out of the body in the home; (2) Ekphora — the funeral procession to the place of burial or cremation; (3) Burial or cremation — the body interred in the earth or burned on a pyre, with grave goods.

The Ekphora and Burial

The second stage was the ekphora — the funeral procession. It took place before dawn, a rule probably intended to prevent excessive public display. The body, on its bier, was carried or transported on a cart to the burial ground, which lay outside the city walls — death was ritually impure and had to be kept apart from the living community. Male relatives walked in the procession; female mourners were often (in Athenian law) restricted to those over sixty or close family, again reflecting attempts to control the scale of display.

The body could be either buried in the earth or cremated, depending on period and local custom. Grave goods — pottery, jewellery, weapons, figurines — were placed in the tomb to accompany the dead. Graves were often marked above ground by stone stelai or sculpted monuments. The stele (plural stelai) typically bore the deceased’s name and sometimes a relief carving. Some of the finest examples survive from classical Athens: the Hegeso Stele (now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens) shows a seated woman receiving a jewellery box from a standing female attendant, rendered with quiet elegance and carved in relief.

A widely attested Greek and Roman practice was placing a coin in the mouth or on the eyes of the deceased. This coin was the fare for Charon, the ferryman who transported souls across the river Styx (or Acheron) to the underworld. Without this payment, the soul could not cross and would be left to wander the bank for a hundred years. Archaeological evidence — coins found in graves in both the Greek and Roman worlds — confirms the literary accounts. The practice is vivid evidence of how Greek and Roman beliefs about the soul’s journey after death shaped funerary behaviour.

Greek Festivals for the Dead: Genesia

The dead were not forgotten after burial. The Genesia was an Athenian public festival in honour of the dead and the ancestors, held annually. Offerings of food and libations were brought to the graves, and the family commemorated their dead together. Private family commemoration of the dead also took place on the third day after death (the trita) and the ninth day (the enata).

Roman Funeral Practices

Roman funerals closely paralleled their Greek counterparts in structure but had distinctively Roman features. The body was washed and prepared by the family, but wealthy Romans could belong to funeral clubs (collegia funeraticia), which guaranteed a proper burial for members who could not afford one independently. The funeral procession in Rome was often elaborate: for a noble Roman, professional mourners (praeficae) were hired, musicians played, and actors wearing the death masks (imagines) of the deceased’s ancestors walked in the procession, creating a living tableau of the family’s lineage.

Roman burial law required interment outside city walls, and the major roads leading out of Rome — especially the Via Appia — were lined with tombs, mausoleums and grave monuments. Romans used both burial and cremation, with cremation becoming fashionable among the elite during the Imperial period before inhumation (burial) returned to favour in the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, partly under the influence of Eastern religions and later Christianity.

Key Fact

The Parentalia (13–21 February) was a period of private commemoration of dead family members, when temples closed, marriages were forbidden, and families visited graves with offerings. The Lemuria (9, 11 and 13 May) was a festival to appease the lemures — restless, potentially harmful spirits of the dead — through a midnight ritual performed by the paterfamilias.

Both cultures shared the belief that the dead required ongoing attention and offerings — neglecting the dead was dangerous as well as impious. The Greek Genesia and the Roman Parentalia served the same basic function: keeping the dead appeased through annual ritual. However, the Roman Lemuria suggests a stronger anxiety about potentially malevolent spirits of the dead returning to harm the living — a belief with no clear Greek parallel at the same level of elaboration. The Roman use of ancestor masks (imagines) in funerary processions was also distinctively Roman, serving the political function of displaying the family’s social prestige and distinguished history.
exam_tip_html: Questions about death and burial often use the command word Describe: “Describe the stages of a Greek funeral.” Give specific named stages — prothesis (laying-out), ekphora (procession), burial/cremation — and for each say what happened and why. The most common mistake is conflating the prothesis with the ekphora or forgetting the role of women in mourning. For source analysis questions involving a stele, always use specific details from the carving: what the figure is shown doing, who is present, the object they hold, and what the relief style suggests about how Greeks wished to commemorate their dead. For an essay comparing Greek and Roman funeral practices, do not just list what each did — explain what the similarities and differences reveal about each culture’s beliefs about the soul, the family, and social status.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Greek funerals followed three stages — prothesis (laying-out), ekphora (procession) and burial or cremation — with ongoing commemoration at the Genesia festival and at family anniversaries; stelai marked graves and served as a public record of the deceased.
  • The custom of placing a coin in the mouth or on the eyes of the dead reflects belief in Charon, the ferryman of the underworld, and reveals how burial rites were directly shaped by beliefs about the soul’s journey after death.
  • Roman festivals for the dead — the Parentalia (February, for family commemoration) and the Lemuria (May, to appease restless spirits) — show that the Roman dead required ongoing ritual attention; the use of ancestor masks in noble funerary processions linked the individual death to the family’s political identity and public prestige.

practice_questions.text: What is the Greek term for the funeral procession that carried the body from the home to the burial ground?
Describe the prothesis stage of a Greek funeral.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: the body was washed and anointed with oil by the women of the household; the body was dressed in grave clothes and laid out on a bier in the entrance hall; the feet pointed towards the door; the body was wreathed with garlands; family and friends gathered to lament; women performed formal ritualised mourning (wailing, beating breasts, tearing hair); the prothesis took place in the home before the ekphora.

practice_questions.text: Consider this description of a carved stone grave monument: a tall stone slab carved in shallow relief, showing a seated woman dressed in elegant drapery who reaches towards an open jewellery box held out to her by a standing female figure; below the scene the woman's name is inscribed. What does this monument tell us about Greek attitudes towards death and commemoration? Use specific details from the description in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Uses multiple specific details (seated woman = the deceased shown in a moment of ordinary life; standing attendant = her slave, suggesting status; jewellery box = personal identity and wealth; shallow relief carving = refined craft honouring the dead; inscribed name = public commemoration of the individual) with sustained analysis of what each implies about Greek attitudes (the desire to remember the dead as they were in life; the importance of status; the role of women in maintaining social memory; the stele as public statement); clear judgement.
Secure (3-4): Two or three details analysed with explanation of significance.
Developing (2): One or two details mentioned with limited analysis.
Emerging (1): General description without engaging with source details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why proper burial was so important in ancient Greek and Roman culture.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following developed points: the unburied dead were believed unable to cross into Hades, condemned to wander for a hundred years; the obligation to bury was a moral and religious duty on the family; without a coin for Charon the soul could not cross the underworld rivers; proper burial kept the dead from becoming restless spirits who might harm the living; burial rites maintained the family's social prestige and public identity; it is illustrated in Sophocles' Antigone where Antigone defies a king's order to ensure her brother's burial.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Greek and Roman approaches to death and burial were essentially the same? Use named sources and a balanced argument in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained balanced argument identifying genuine similarities (both required burial outside city walls; both had ritual laying-out of the body; both used grave goods; both had festivals for the dead; both placed coins for Charon) alongside real differences (Roman funeral clubs for the poor with no Greek equivalent; Roman use of ancestor masks in processions; Lemuria specifically for malevolent spirits vs Genesia for honoured ancestors; Roman cremation was an elite fashion linked to Imperial period; stelai in Greece vs elaborate roadside tombs and mausoleums in Rome); evidence from named sources (Sophocles' Antigone, the Hegeso Stele, Parentalia and Lemuria); clear judgement.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument with evidence for similarities and differences and a conclusion.
Developing (3-5): Points about one side with limited comparison or source use.
Emerging (1-2): Descriptive account; little argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Roman festivals for the dead differed from the Greek festival of the Genesia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Lemuria aimed at appeasing potentially harmful lemures/spirits vs Genesia as a respectful commemoration of honoured ancestors; Parentalia as a private family event with public ceremonies at graves vs Genesia as a public festival; Roman civic dimension of the Parentalia with public ceremonies and closure of temples vs Genesia as primarily a family affair; the duration of Parentalia — nine days — vs the Genesia which was a single-day event) each with named evidence and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about Roman vs Greek attitudes to the dead.
Secure (3-4): Two differences explained with some evidence.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the prothesis in a Greek funeral?
options: The procession carrying the body from the home to the burial ground
The coin placed in the dead person's mouth as the ferryman's fare
The preparation and public laying-out of the body in the home
The carved stone grave marker inscribed with the deceased's name

knowledge_checks.q: In Greek and Roman belief, Charon required a coin as payment to do what?
options: Guard the entrance to the underworld
Ferry the soul across the river Styx to the underworld
Judge whether the soul deserved to enter Elysium
Provide grave goods for the journey after death

knowledge_checks.q: The second stage of a Greek funeral, in which the body was carried in procession to the place of burial, was called the _____.
The Roman festival held in February to commemorate dead family members, during which graves were visited with offerings, was called the _____.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: An upright stone grave marker, often inscribed with the deceased's name and sometimes carved with a relief scene
An Athenian annual public festival in honour of the dead and the ancestors
Roman associations that paid regular dues to guarantee their members a proper burial

flashcard_questions.a: Associations whose members paid regular dues to guarantee themselves and their families a proper burial.

flashcard_questions.a: A Roman May festival to appease lemures — restless, potentially harmful spirits of the dead.

flashcard_questions.a: Antigone, in which the heroine defies the king's edict to ensure her brother receives proper burial.

glossary_terms.definition: The first stage of a Greek funeral: the preparation and public laying-out of the body in the home, with the family gathering to mourn around it.
The second stage of a Greek funeral: the procession that carried the body from the home to the place of burial or cremation, typically held before dawn.
An upright stone grave marker, often inscribed with the name of the deceased and sometimes carved with a relief scene showing the person in life.
In Greek myth, the ferryman of the dead who transported souls across the river Styx (or Acheron) to the underworld, requiring payment of a coin placed in the mouth or on the eyes of the deceased.
An Athenian annual public festival held in honour of the dead and the ancestors, at which offerings were made at graves.
Roman associations whose members paid regular dues to guarantee a proper funeral and burial for themselves and their families, particularly among the poor and slave populations.
